title: Edmund Burke

cards.b: Edmund Burke (1729-97), Irish-born Whig MP, is the father of modern conservatism, but his thought is wider: a theory of representation, party and empire as well. He wrote as a practising politician, and UPSC likes his views on the French Revolution, rights, representation, and his role in the impeachment of Warren Hastings.

cards.h: Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)
cards.b:
Burke attacked the Revolution for its abstract rights, rationalism and violence. Rights of men exist, but they are 'the rights of Englishmen': inherited and practical, not metaphysical. He feared the destruction of church, monarchy and property would yield terror and a military despot, a prophecy credited with Napoleon.

'Society is a partnership... between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.'

Institutions gain authority by long use (prescription). 'Prejudice' means stored wisdom, not mere bias. Change must come by 'preserving and improving' what exists, as in the Glorious Revolution of 1688, which he praised as a conservative act. He backed the American colonists in 1775-83 because they defended their traditional liberties.

In his Speech to the Electors of Bristol (1774), Burke held that an MP is a trustee, not a delegate: 'Your representative owes you not his industry only, but his judgment.' Parliament is a deliberative body for the whole nation.

In Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770) he defined party as 'a body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle'. This is an early defence of party as principled, not factional.

Burke led the impeachment of Warren Hastings, Governor-General of Bengal (1773-85), tried before the House of Lords from 1788; Hastings was acquitted in 1795. Burke charged him with corruption and cruelty (Rohilla war, Chait Singh, Begums of Awadh) and argued that power over India was a trust held for Indians' welfare, answerable to a higher moral law. He also noted Indian civilisation had ancient laws and institutions that must be respected.

• Paine, Rights of Man (1791) and Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790): inherited privilege is injustice.
  • Tradition defends oppression such as slavery and caste.
  • His romance with chivalry and aristocracy was out of date.
  • Radicals: contradictory to back America but oppose France.
  • Defenders: a prophet of the dangers of ideological politics.

He links Locke's liberty with later conservatives: Oakeshott, Hayek on 'spontaneous order' and Scruton. He is also quoted by those on the left for the defence of community. A Burkean can be a liberal, a Whig, or a traditionalist. Compare Rousseau's will and Bentham's calculus, which Burke would have called abstract.

Burke's Hastings speeches shaped the idea of accountable empire, later the Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784) debates. Indian moderates like Dadabhai Naoroji and Gokhale used Burke's 'trust' idea to demand that British rule serve Indians. Constitution-makers' gradualism and the keeping of inherited institutions resemble Burkean caution.

Structure: context, Reflections, tradition, representation, party, Hastings, critique, India.

Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) is the key text, and his Speech to the Electors of Bristol (1774) states the trustee view of representation.

His 1775 Speech on Conciliation with America shows his preference for practical concession over abstract rights.
